![](feature.gif){fig-alt="The keys of a typewriter with \"R\" highlighted and the word \"plot\" being typed"}

One could think of data science as "art grounded in facts". It tells a story through visualisation. Both story and visualisation rely on a good plot. And an abundance of those has evolved over time. Many have their own dedicated Wikipedia page {{< iconify iconoir emoji-surprise-alt >}}.

Which generate the most interest? How is the interest trending over time? Let's build an interactive serverless Shiny app to find out.

```{r}
#| label: article-setup

library(ggfoundry)
library(usedthese)
```

```{r}
#| label: libraries

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)
library(purrr)
library(stringr)
library(tibble)
library(shiny)
library(bslib)
library(rvest)
library(scales)
library(httr2)
library(wesanderson)
```

```{r}
#| label: app-theme

theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 11))

pal <- wes_palette(8, name = "IsleofDogs1", type = "continuous")
```

```{r}
#| label: palette
#| dev.args: { bg: "transparent" }

display_palette(pal, "wesanderson::IsleofDogs1")
```

I'm going to start by harvesting some data from Wikipedia's [Statistical charts and diagrams category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category:Statistical_charts_and_diagrams). I can use this to build a list of all chart types which have a dedicated Wikipedia article page. Using rvest [@rvest] inside the app ensures it will respond to any newly-created articles.

```{r}
#| label: scrape

charts <-
  tibble(
    chart = read_html(str_c(
      "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/",
      "Category:Statistical_charts_and_diagrams"
    )) |>
      html_elements(".mw-category-group a") |>
      html_text()
  )
```

The page-view data comes from the Wikimedia API. A function wrapped around {httr2} [@httr2] calls the endpoint directly, so I can later iterate through a subset of the list established in the prior code chunk. This replaces the {pageviews} package, which has no WebAssembly build -- a detail that matters now the app runs in the browser rather than on a server.

```{r}
#| label: pageview

pv <- function(article, end_date = today()) {
  request("https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/metrics/pageviews/per-article") |>
    req_url_path_append(
      "en.wikipedia",
      "all-access",
      "user",
      URLencode(article, reserved = TRUE),
      "daily",
      "2015070100",
      str_c(format(end_date, "%Y%m%d"), "00")
    ) |>
    req_perform() |>
    resp_body_json(simplify = TRUE) |>
    pluck("items") |>
    as_tibble() |>
    mutate(date = ymd(str_sub(timestamp, 1, 8))) |>
    select(article, date, views)
}
```

I want an input selector so that a user can choose plot types for comparison. I also want to provide user control of the y-axis scale. A combination of *fixed* and *log10* is better for comparing plots. *Free* scaling reveals more detail in the individual trends.

The UI was originally laid out with {gridlayout}. It is now built with {bslib} [@shiny]'s own `page_sidebar()`, which has the happy side-effect that every package in the app has a pre-built WebAssembly binary. The title-bar logo is now the tracked asset [www/logo.png](www/logo.png).

```{r}
#| label: ui

logo <- "logo.png"

ui <- bslib::page(
  theme = bs_theme(
    bootswatch = "simplex",
    primary = "#9986A5",
    font_scale = 0.95
  ),
  tags$style(
    ".app-title {
      display: flex;
      justify-content: center;
      align-items: center;
      gap: 0.5rem;
      padding: 0.5rem 0;
      font-size: 1.1rem;
    }
    .controls {
      padding: 0.75rem 1rem;
    }
    .card-header {
      padding: 0.5rem 0.75rem;
    }
    .card-body {
      padding: 0.75rem;
    }
    .shiny-input-container {
      margin-bottom: 0.75rem;
    }
    .control-label {
      margin-bottom: 0.15rem;
    }"
  ),
  tags$header(
    tags$img(src = logo, height = "32px", alt = "Plot Plotter logo"),
    "Plot Plotter",
    class = "app-title"
  ),
  div(
    class = "controls",
    layout_columns(
      col_widths = c(6, 6),
    dateRangeInput("dates",
      label = "Date range",
      start = "2015-07-01",
      end = NULL
    ),
    selectizeInput(
      inputId = "article",
      label = "Chart type",
      choices = charts$chart,
      selected = c(
        "Violin plot",
        "Dendrogram",
        "Histogram",
        "Pie chart",
        "Q–Q plot",
        "Error bar"
      ),
      options = list(maxItems = 6),
      multiple = TRUE
    ),
    selectInput(
      inputId = "scales",
      label = "Fixed or free y-axis",
      choices = c("Fixed" = "fixed", "Free" = "free"),
      selected = "fixed"
    ),
    selectInput(
      inputId = "log10",
      label = "Log 10 or normal y-axis",
      choices = c("Log 10" = "log10", "Normal" = "norm"),
      selected = "log10"
    )
    )
  ),
  card(
    full_screen = TRUE,
    plotOutput("line")
  )
)
```

The server component outputs a faceted ggplot.

```{r}
#| label: server

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  pv_cached <- memoise::memoise(
    pv,
    cache = cachem::cache_mem(
      max_size = 32 * 1024^2,
      max_age = 3600
    )
  )

  pv_history <- reactive({
    req(input$article)
    end_date <- today()
    input$article |>
      map(pv_cached, end_date = end_date) |>
      list_rbind() |>
      mutate(article = str_replace_all(article, "_", " "))
  })

  pv_df <- reactive({
    pv_history() |>
      dplyr::filter(date >= input$dates[1], date <= input$dates[2])
  })

  output$line <- renderPlot({
    p <- ggplot(
      pv_df(),
      aes(date, views, colour = article)
    ) +
      geom_line() +
      geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, colour = pal[7]) +
      scale_colour_manual(values = pal) +
      facet_wrap(~article, ncol = 3, scales = input$scales) +
      theme(
        legend.position = "none",
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 8),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 9),
        plot.margin = margin(5, 10, 5, 10, "pt"),
        plot.caption = element_text(size = 8, hjust = 0)
      ) +
      labs(
        x = NULL, y = NULL,
        caption = "Source: Daily Wikipedia Article Page Views"
      )

    switch(input$log10,
      norm = p,
      log10 = p + scale_y_log10(
        labels = label_number(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())
      )
    )
  })
}
```

```{r}
#| label: app-run
#| include: false

shinyApp(ui, server)
```

The serverless app below is embedded using the {shinylive} [@shinylive] Quarto extension. A small hidden chunk assembles the app chunks above and emits it for the {shinylive} filter. R and {shiny} run in your browser via WebR, without a hosted R server. An internet connection is still needed to load the runtime and packages and retrieve Wikipedia data. The first load can take a little time.

```{r}
#| label: app-embed
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
#| cache: false

app_code <-
  c("libraries", "scrape", "pageview", "app-theme", "ui", "server", "app-run") |>
  map(knitr::knit_code$get) |>
  unlist()

writeLines(
  c(
    "```{shinylive-r}",
    "#| standalone: true",
    "#| components: [viewer]",
    "#| viewerHeight: 700",
    "",
    app_code,
    "",
    "## file: www/logo.png",
    "## type: binary",
    "{{< base64 www/logo.png >}}",
    "```"
  )
)
```

Note the utility of selecting the right scaling. The combination of "fixed" and "normal" reveals what must have been "world histogram day" on July 27th 2015, but little else.

Turning non-interactive code into an app sharpens the mind's focus on performance. And profvis [@profvis], integrated into RStudio via the profile menu option, is a wonderful "tool for helping you understand how R spends its time".

My first version of the app was finger-tappingly slow.

Profvis revealed the main culprit to be the pre-loading of a dataframe with the page-view data for all chart types (there are more than 100). Profiling prompted the more efficient "reactive" approach of loading the data only for the user's selection (maximum of 8).

Profiling also showed that rounding the corners of the plot.background with additional grid-package code was expensive. App efficiency felt more important than minor cosmetic detailing (to the main panel to match the theme's side panel). And most users would probably barely notice (had I not drawn attention to it here).
